works.title: The Crucifixion of Saint Andrew
works.alt: Caravaggio painting: an old man bound to a cross in deep shadow, an executioner on a ladder reaching up toward the ropes with his arms raised, onlookers below lit from the left.
works.label: Painted in Naples, in the months after Caravaggio fled Rome under sentence of death for killing a man. The legend holds that Andrew preached from the cross for two days until the crowd demanded his release, and that the executioner sent to cut him down found his hands would not move. That is the instant here: the man on the ladder, arms up, stopped.

works.title: Island of the Dead
works.alt: Böcklin painting: a small rowing boat carrying a white shrouded figure and a draped coffin approaches a rocky island walled with stone, a grove of black cypresses rising at its center.
works.label: The island exists nowhere. A young widow commissioned the picture as a memorial to her husband, and the draped coffin and the white standing figure were added at her request. Cliffs and cypresses drop to near-silhouette, so the only truly lit thing in the painting is the small boat. This is the first of five versions Böcklin painted; the one usually reproduced online is the 1883 Berlin picture.

works.title: The Beacons of Gondor
works.label: Nearly ten feet across, painted in traditional oils from posed models rather than digitally. The beacon fire is the only warm light in the picture, so the whole composition is built out of how far that light carries before it gives out.

works.title: The Harvesters
works.alt: Bruegel painting: a golden wheat field in late summer, peasants cutting a path through the standing corn while others eat and one sleeps beneath a pear tree, a village and bay beyond.
works.label: One of six panels Bruegel painted for a wealthy Antwerp merchant, marking the turns of the year; five survive. It is among the earliest European paintings to treat ordinary labor as a subject worth the whole canvas rather than a detail at the edge of a religious scene. The wheat is waist-high and the cut path through it leads the eye straight back to the village.

works.title: Hen and Rooster with Grapevine
works.medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk, image 101.9 × 41.3 cm
works.alt: Jakuchū hanging scroll: a rooster with a long arching tail and a hen beneath a grapevine heavy with fruit, painted in ink and color on silk.
works.label: Jakuchū ran his family's Kyoto greengrocery for forty years before handing it over to paint full time, and he was seventy-six when he made this. The bird is assembled from hundreds of separate feather strokes rather than massed shapes, and its tail is drawn crossing in front of the grapevine instead of disappearing behind it.

works.title: Ghosts of the Taira at Daimotsu Bay
works.medium: Triptych of woodblock prints (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
works.alt: Kuniyoshi woodblock triptych: a sailing ship crowded with armored warriors rides a towering blue wave, while the ghosts of drowned Taira soldiers rise out of the sea around it.
works.label: Yoshitsune's ship driven into Daimotsu Bay by a storm and set upon by the ghosts of the Taira warriors drowned at Dan-no-ura — the clan his own campaign destroyed. Kuniyoshi returned to the subject more than once. It is a triptych: three separate sheets, designed to hang together so the wave runs unbroken across all three.

works.title: Twilight in the Wilderness
works.alt: Church painting: a wilderness sky at sunset burning orange and crimson in long streaked clouds, above dark silent hills, a river and a line of firs with no people anywhere in it.
works.label: Painted the year before the Civil War began, from studies Church made in Maine, and emptied of every human figure — no cabin, no boat, no road. Almost half the canvas is sky. The red is laid in thin glazes over a pale ground so the clouds appear lit from behind rather than colored on the surface.

works.title: Madame X (Virginie Amélie Avegno Gautreau)
works.alt: Sargent portrait: a woman in a black full-length gown with jeweled straps stands in profile against a dark brown ground, one hand resting on a small table, her skin painted pale lavender-gray.
works.label: The 1884 Paris Salon received it so badly that Sargent left for London and stayed. Gautreau powdered her skin with lavender, and Sargent matched it exactly, which is why she reads almost gray against the black dress and brown ground. The right strap originally hung off her shoulder; he repainted it upright after the Salon, and the picture stayed in his studio for thirty years.

works.title: The Crucifixion
works.medium: Tempera on wood, gold ground, 63.8 × 48.3 cm
works.alt: Fra Angelico panel: Christ on the cross against a flat gold ground, small blue-winged angels in the gold around him, a crowd of soldiers in red caps and riders on horseback below, and the Virgin collapsing in blue while the Marys kneel in pink at the foot of the cross.
works.label: An early panel, small enough that the Metropolitan takes it to have been made for private devotion rather than for an altar. Mourners, soldiers and mounted riders close in a ring around the foot of the cross, a circular arrangement the museum traces to Lorenzo Ghiberti's bronze doors for the Florence Baptistery. Behind the cross there is no sky at all, only gold.

works.title: Icon of the Mother of God and Infant Christ (Virgin Eleousa)
works.medium: Tempera and gold on wood, 96 × 70 cm
works.alt: Cretan icon: the Virgin in a deep red mantle presses her cheek against the infant Christ, who wears a pale blue tunic under a gold-orange wrap and holds a scroll, both set against a worn gold ground.
works.label: Painted on Crete while the island was under Venetian rule, and large enough to have stood on an iconostasis, the screen that closes off the sanctuary in a Greek Orthodox church. The Eleousa, or tenderness, type puts mother and child cheek to cheek rather than facing the congregation straight on. Cleveland gives the panel to Angelos Akotantos, the most sought-after painter in Candia, as an attribution rather than a signature.

works.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx
works.alt: Moreau painting: a sphinx with a woman's head, a lion's body and blue and white wings clings by her claws to the chest of a standing nude Oedipus, the two locked eye to eye on a narrow rock ledge, with a dead man's foot and hand showing at the lower edge.
works.label: Moreau made his name with this picture at the Paris Salon of 1864, at a moment when French painting was turning toward scenes of ordinary modern life. He went the other way, into myth, and a younger generation that included Odilon Redon and Oscar Wilde followed him there. The sphinx has jumped and is holding on by her claws: the riddle is being put at close range, and what is left of the travelers who answered wrong lies on the ledge below.

works.title: The Books of Earthsea: The Complete Illustrated Edition
works.medium: More than fifty color and black-and-white illustrations
works.label: Four years of work, made in close collaboration with Ursula K. Le Guin, who chose the scenes herself and died months before the book appeared. The dragon alone took about a year of revision, each sketch pulling it further from a reptile and closer to a face. Vess keeps the figures small inside large landscapes, so it is the islands rather than the wizards that carry the pictures.

works.title: Blind Orion Searching for the Rising Sun
works.alt: Poussin landscape: the giant Orion strides through a wooded valley with one arm outstretched, a small man riding on his shoulders to point the way and another small figure watching from below, while a woman stands on a dark cloud above him.
works.label: Orion, blinded, walking east toward the sunrise that is to give him back his sight, with Cedalion riding his shoulders to steer him and Hephaestus watching from below. Diana stands on the storm cloud that hangs across his eyes; one long-standing reading takes her presence as notice of the death she will later deal him. Poussin painted it in Rome in 1658 for Michel Passart, a Paris finance official who owned at least seven of his pictures.

works.title: Nur Jahan holding a portrait of Emperor Jahangir
works.medium: Gum tempera and gold on paper; painting 13.6 × 6.4 cm, page 30 × 22.1 cm
works.alt: Mughal album page: a woman in a white striped skirt and orange veil stands barefoot in profile on a plain green ground, holding up a small framed portrait of the bearded emperor, the whole page set in a wide border of white blossoms on dark blue.
works.label: Nur Jahan was the emperor Jahangir's favorite wife and ran much of the business of the state in his name. She holds his portrait here after his death, shown in an idealized youth — she was about fifty when he died — while he appears aged behind the rail that marked imperial presence. The painting itself is only about five inches tall; everything outside that narrow panel is the album border.

works.title: Streams and Mountains
works.medium: Hanging scroll; ink on paper, image 92.2 × 37.6 cm
works.alt: Chinese hanging scroll in ink: a mountain mass built from dense fine strokes rises the full height of the sheet, trees and a thatched retreat beside a stream at the bottom, columns of inscription across the top and red collectors' seals at the edges.
works.label: Painted during one of the stretches Xu Ben spent in retreat from official life, in the years when the Yuan dynasty was giving way to the Ming. The mountain is built almost entirely from repeated hemp-fiber strokes, so the rock reads as one continuous rhythm rather than as separate masses stacked up. At the base, a scholar comes up through the trees on foot toward the hermit's house.

works.title: Wheat Fields
works.alt: Ruisdael landscape: a broad sandy track runs between pale ripening wheat fields toward a stand of trees and a few low roofs, two small figures walking on the path, with a tall bank of cumulus filling more than half the sky.
works.label: More than half the canvas is given to the clouds, and the land below is arranged to serve them: the track widens as it comes forward, and the two figures on it are small enough to set the scale of everything else. The wheat is pale and nearly ready to cut. Ruisdael and his generation worked the horizon this low so that weather could be the real subject of a landscape.

works.title: The Birth of Venus
works.alt: Cabanel painting: a nude Venus lies stretched full length along the crest of a green wave, her long auburn hair trailing in the water and one arm raised across her eyes, while a flight of winged cherubs crosses the pale sky above her, two of them blowing conch shells.
works.label: This is the Metropolitan's picture, painted in 1875 for the New York collector John Wolfe; the first and slightly larger version made a sensation at the Salon of 1863, was bought by Napoleon III, and is now in the Musée d'Orsay. Cabanel finishes the sea as smoothly as the figure and leaves no visible brushwork anywhere, which is precisely what the next generation of French painters would attack. Venus does not stand on a shell here but lies along the wave, arm across her face, somewhere between waking and not.

works.title: Young Woman Knitting
works.alt: Morisot painting: a young woman in a straw hat and pale jacket sits knitting on a slatted garden chair beside a flowering border, a second empty chair standing on the gravel path at the right, the whole picture brushed in loose strokes of green, cream and pink.
works.label: Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionist group and showed in all but one of its eight exhibitions. The paint is left open here — the gravel path and the empty chair are barely more than dragged strokes over the ground — and the hands, the one part of the picture actually doing work, are the least finished thing in it. Her signature sits at the lower left in the same thin paint as the garden.

works.title: Plum Garden at Kamata
works.medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper, 33.7 × 21.9 cm
works.alt: Japanese woodblock print: bare plum trunks in the foreground, white blossom filling the middle distance, and a flat graded red sky behind, with small figures on a path below.
works.label: One of the hundred views Hiroshige made of Edo and its outskirts in the last years of his life. Kamata, south of the city, was somewhere people travelled to specifically to see the plums in flower, and the print is built around that: trunks in the near ground, blossom across the middle, and the rest given over to a flat sky laid in as a graded wash. The red is as much the subject as the trees are.

works.title: Black-naped Oriole Perched on a Stem of Rose Mallow
works.medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper, 37.3 × 12.5 cm
works.alt: Narrow upright Japanese print: a yellow oriole grips a mallow stem across the middle of the sheet, a single orange flower open at the bottom, against a pale ground.
works.label: A bird-and-flower print in the tall narrow format cut to hang on a pillar, which is why it is barely a hand across and more than a foot down. The shape does the work: the stem enters at the top, the bird hangs off it at the middle, the flower opens at the foot, and the eye has to travel the full drop of the sheet. Hiroshige made these by the hundred alongside the landscapes he is better known for.

works.title: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt
works.alt: Panel painting: the Virgin in a deep blue robe sits on a rock in a wooded landscape nursing the Christ child, with a path, small distant figures and a town beyond the trees.
works.label: The subject is a rest stop on the journey out of Judea, and David sets it in a Netherlandish wood — oaks, a worn path, a town in the distance — rather than anywhere near Egypt. The Virgin takes the whole center of the panel, in a blue that would have been the most expensive material in it. Small figures keep the journey going in the background, so the picture holds the pause and the road at the same time.

works.title: Pandora
works.alt: Tall oil painting: a pale nude figure holding a box stands among loosely painted flowers in reds, blues and yellows, under a blue sky and bare branches.
works.label: Redon spent the first half of his career working almost entirely in black, in charcoal and lithography, and the second half in color; this belongs to the end of the second. Pandora holds the box, but the myth is barely the point — the flowers get more attention than she does, scattered in the loose patches of color he used in his flower paintings. He was in his seventies when he painted it.

works.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
works.medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper, 25.7 × 37.9 cm
works.alt: Japanese woodblock print: a huge breaking wave with clawed foam fills the left and arches over three low boats, with the small snow-capped cone of Mount Fuji beyond.
works.label: From Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and the reason most people outside Japan can picture a Hokusai at all. Fuji is in it, small, sitting under the break of the wave — the mountain is the whole point of the series and here it is nearly upstaged. The blue is Prussian blue, imported and by the 1830s cheap enough to print in quantity, which is a good part of why the series looks the way it does.

works.title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
works.alt: A bearded man in a black smock, wide dark hat and gold chain stands in shadow, resting one hand on a pale marble bust of a blind bearded head.
works.label: Painted for a Sicilian collector who wanted a philosopher and left the subject to Rembrandt. Aristotle rests a hand on Homer, who was poor and blind, while the gold chain over his own shoulder is the kind a ruler gives a courtier — the picture sets what a thinker is paid against what a poet was worth. Almost everything is black or brown except the white sleeve and the bust, and the light falls only where Rembrandt wants the question asked.

works.title: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
works.alt: A woman in a white linen headcloth, blue skirt and black bodice stands at a table, one hand on a leaded window and the other on a silver pitcher in a basin, a map on the wall behind her.
works.label: She is doing two things at once and neither is finished: opening the window with her left hand, lifting the pitcher with her right. Vermeer builds the whole picture out of that pause. Light comes through the leaded glass and lands blue on the white linen, and the map on the back wall is the kind Dutch households actually hung. The first Vermeer to enter an American public collection, in 1889.

works.title: The Penitent Magdalen
works.alt: A seated woman in a white blouse and dark skirt, a red cloth across her lap, rests both hands on a skull and looks toward a candle whose flame is doubled in an ornate mirror.
works.label: One of several Magdalens La Tour painted; this is the Met's, sometimes called the Magdalen with Two Flames for the candle and its reflection. The jewelry is pushed to the edge of the table and the skull sits in her lap instead, which is the whole argument of the picture made without a word. La Tour was forgotten for most of three centuries and only rebuilt into the canon after 1915.

works.title: Two Men Contemplating the Moon
works.alt: Two men in long coats stand with their backs turned on a rocky path at dusk, looking at a thin crescent moon, under a leaning uprooted oak with bare branches.
works.label: The figures have their backs to the viewer, which is Friedrich's habit: you are put behind them and made to look at what they are looking at rather than at them. The dead oak leaning over the path and the small evergreen beside it were read by his contemporaries as a pairing of the old faith and the new. He painted the subject more than once; this is the Met's version, and the men wear old German dress, which was a political costume in Saxony at the time.

works.title: View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm—The Oxbow
works.alt: A wide river valley seen from a height: storm clouds and dark broken trees fill the left side, while on the right the Connecticut River loops through sunlit cleared farmland.
works.label: The canvas is split down the middle — wilderness and storm on the left, cleared and farmed valley on the right — and Cole puts himself at the bottom center, a tiny figure at an easel looking back at the viewer. He painted it in a few months to show at the National Academy and to argue a case about what settlement was doing to the American landscape. The umbrella and portfolio beside him are the only things in the picture that admit a person made it.

works.title: Julie Le Brun (1780–1819) Looking in a Mirror
works.alt: A girl in a green dress and white headscarf holds up a red-framed mirror in profile; her reflected face looks straight out of the glass at the viewer.
works.label: The painter's daughter, about seven, holding a mirror. Vigée Le Brun gives her two faces at once — the real child in profile, the reflection turned out to meet the viewer — so the picture is both a portrait and a small argument about what a portrait is. It was painted in 1787, two years before the Revolution sent her out of France; she spent twelve years working in Italy, Austria and Russia before she came back.

works.title: Pygmalion and Galatea
works.alt: In a sculptor's studio, a nude female figure on a low stand twists down to kiss a man in a blue tunic; her legs are still white marble while her upper body has turned to flesh. A winged cupid aims an arrow from the upper right.
works.label: Gérôme painted this subject several times; the Met's version shows the figure from behind, with the change from stone to flesh caught partway up her legs. He was a sculptor as well as a painter and made a marble of the same pair, so the studio around them — the turntable, the wooden steps, the mallet on the floor — is his own. The masks hanging on the back wall are a reminder that the whole thing is staged.

works.title: Snowscape with Figures
works.medium: Hanging scroll; ink on silk, 53 × 67.3 cm (painting only)
works.alt: Ink painting on darkened silk: a snow-covered bluff with bare trees and a small roofed pavilion at the left, water opening out to low distant hills, a tiny boat at the right, and an inscription with a red seal in the upper left corner.
works.label: Dated by its own inscription to 1584 and signed by Kim Si, a Joseon painter who worked in the manner of the Chinese Zhe school and was known for winter scenes. The snow is not painted; it is the untouched silk, with the ink laid in around it, so the brightest thing in the picture is the part the brush never reached. The silk has darkened over four centuries, which has narrowed the contrast the painter was working with.

works.title: Return of the King of the Dead
works.label: Whelan calls this a sequel to his own cover for Michael Moorcock's The Bane of the Black Sword, painted decades later and on his own account rather than to a commission. It is small — twelve inches by nine — and in acrylic on panel, which is close quarters for a picture holding an armored giant and a swordsman. He has said it was mostly done as a goof, while adding that the symbolism in it is deliberate.

works.title: Cypresses
works.alt: Two dark cypress trees fill most of the canvas, their branches twisting upward in thick curling brushstrokes against a pale sky with a crescent moon; wheat and flowering shrubs run along the bottom.
works.label: Painted at Saint-Rémy in the summer of 1889, a few weeks after Van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum there. He had been circling the cypress for months, writing to his brother that nobody had yet painted one the way he saw it, and that its proportions were those of an Egyptian obelisk. The paint is laid on thickly enough to cast its own shadows, so the tree reads as carved as much as painted.

works.title: Icon of the Virgin and Child, Hodegetria variant
works.alt: A small painted panel of the Virgin holding the Christ child on her left arm, her right hand raised toward him; both wear deep red and gold robes against a gold ground.
works.label: Hodegetria means she who shows the way, and names the gesture: the Virgin’s free hand points to the child rather than to herself. The type was copied for centuries from a lost icon in Constantinople said to have been painted from life. This panel is small enough to hold, and was made in the eastern Mediterranean during the Crusader period, when Byzantine and Western workshops were working side by side and not always separably.

works.title: Cover of Amazing Stories, July 1927
works.medium: Color process printing on pulp paper
works.alt: A pulp magazine cover: a woman in a white gown lies curled inside a huge transparent egg-shaped shell on a rocky shore, while a man in a red tunic stands over her; the magazine title runs in heavy orange letters across the top.
works.label: Paul drew nearly every cover of Amazing Stories in its first years, and largely invented how science fiction looked before anyone had agreed what it was. He was trained as an architect and draftsman, which shows in the machinery: the hardware is drawn as though it could be built, and the people are there mostly to give it scale. This issue carried the second installment of A. Merritt’s The Moon Pool.

works.title: Mona Lisa
works.alt: A seated woman turned three quarters toward the viewer, hands folded one over the other, in front of a winding river valley of blue-green hills that sit at different heights on either side of her.
works.label: Leonardo kept the panel for the rest of his life and took it with him to France, which is why it is in Paris rather than Florence. The landscape behind her is doing quiet work: the horizon on the left sits lower than the one on the right, so the eye keeps resettling and her expression seems to change with it. The surface carries almost no visible brushwork, built instead from glazes laid so thinly that the transitions have no edges at all.

works.title: Juan de Pareja
works.artist: Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez)
works.alt: A man in a dark doublet with a wide white collar, turned three quarters toward the viewer, one hand at his hip, standing against a plain gray-green ground.
works.label: Velázquez painted this in Rome, partly as a warm-up before he began the portrait of Pope Innocent X, and showed it publicly at the Pantheon that March to considerable noise. The sitter was his own assistant, enslaved in his household; within months Velázquez signed the papers that freed him, and Pareja went on working as a painter in his own right. Almost everything in the picture is a gray-brown, so the white collar and the one lit edge of the cheek are left carrying all of it.

works.title: The Titan's Goblet
works.alt: An enormous stone goblet standing in a landscape, a sea with sailing ships held inside its rim and tiny classical buildings along the inner shore, with hills, a river and a sunset far below.
works.label: Cole never explained it and nobody since has settled it. The rim of the goblet holds a sea of its own, with ships on it, a Greek temple on one shore and a palace on the other, while below the stem an ordinary landscape carries on as though nothing were standing in it. Readings have reached for Norse myth, for Greek myth, and for the painter's own dreams. It is also a small painting — nineteen inches by sixteen — which makes the scale inside it stranger than a large one would.

works.title: The Sermon on the Mount
works.institution: Museum of National History at Frederiksborg Castle
works.alt: Christ seated on a rock with one hand raised, a crowd of listeners spread on the rocks below and around him, several seen from behind, pale hills and a wide sky beyond.
works.label: One of twenty-three scenes from the life of Christ that Bloch painted for the King's Oratory in the chapel at Frederiksborg Castle, a commission that ran from 1865 to 1879 and that the castle's museum still holds. The surrounding crowd tells most of the story. The people are set on either side of Christ. Several of the listeners have their backs turned, most likely showing the viewer of the art sees the sermon from the back rather than the front. Catalogue details for the series travel unevenly through reproduction — the support and measurements here are the ones given most often rather than ones the museum publishes.

works.title: The Fairy Tale Prince
works.alt: A crowned figure in a long rose-red cloak over a patterned robe, standing in deep snow with a sword at his side and dark snow-laden firs behind, while a small shaggy troll in a red cap stands at his feet with one finger raised, talking.
works.label: The signature in the corner is certain. Almost nothing else is. Print sellers list it as The Fairy Tale Prince — Sagoprinsen — but Bukowskis attaches that same title to a different Bauer altogether, a young nobleman with a white horse and no snow in sight, while other listings give only “from a Christmas book, ca. 1907” and decline to name which book. Bauer drew for the Swedish Christmas annuals every year in that stretch, so an annual is the likely answer and may well stay only likely. The content of the image here is simpler than the history surrounding it: a crown, a long cloak, deep snow, and a troll barely waist-high who is entirely unimpressed.

works.title: Jewels from the Deep
works.alt: A sea shown in cross-section: above the waterline two small figures ride a shell boat on a wave under heaped clouds, and far below a mermaid rises through deep green water holding up a shell heaped with jewels toward a hand reaching down to her.
works.label: Catalogued only as Jewels from the Deep, 1909 — which is the year Rackham's Undine appeared and the obvious guess, except that the first edition's own list of fifteen plates does not include it. Historians still are uncertain of the book it belonged to, if it did at all. The method is the usual Rackham: a pen line laid down first and watercolor washed over it in thin coats, which is why the figures look drawn and the water looks stained.
